subject: DBMS
title: What is a DBMS?
learn: A database is organized data; a DBMS is software that stores, retrieves, updates, secures, and manages that data. Examples include PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, and SQL Server. A DBMS gives applications a consistent interface instead of making every program manage files itself.
example: A college app stores students, courses, and marks. The application sends SQL such as SELECT * FROM students WHERE id=10. The DBMS finds the rows, checks permissions, executes the query, and returns the result.
keyPoints: Data is persistent and shared.
DBMS provides querying, concurrency, security, recovery, and integrity.
RDBMS stores data in related tables and commonly uses SQL.

interview.q: DBMS vs file system?
interview.a: A DBMS provides structured querying, constraints, transactions, concurrency control, recovery, indexing, and access control. A basic file system leaves much of this to application code.

mcq.q: Which is primarily a DBMS responsibility?
mcq.why: The DBMS coordinates concurrent operations and transactions.

subject: DBMS
title: Primary, candidate, foreign and composite keys
learn: A super key uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal super key. The primary key is the candidate key chosen as the main identifier. A foreign key references a key in another table and enforces referential integrity. A composite key uses multiple columns together.
example: STUDENT(student_id, email, name) can have candidate keys student_id and email. If ENROLLMENT(student_id, course_id) identifies one enrollment, its primary key can be the composite pair (student_id, course_id).
keyPoints: Primary keys should identify rows uniquely.
Foreign keys model relationships between tables.
Candidate keys are minimal; super keys need not be minimal.

interview.q: Can a table have multiple candidate keys?
interview.a: Yes. It can have several candidate keys but normally one primary key. The other candidate keys can be declared UNIQUE.

mcq.q: What does a foreign key primarily enforce?
mcq.why: It restricts references to valid parent-key values, subject to the constraint definition.

subject: DBMS
title: Entities, attributes and cardinality
learn: An entity is a real-world object represented by data. Attributes describe it. Relationships connect entities. Cardinality describes how many instances can participate: one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many.
example: One department can have many employees, while each employee belongs to one department: Department 1:N Employee. A student can take many courses and a course can have many students: Student M:N Course, usually represented with an Enrollment table.
keyPoints: M:N relationships normally need a junction/associative table in a relational design.
Optionality answers whether participation is required.
Good modeling prevents duplicated and contradictory data.

interview.q: How do you convert M:N to tables?
interview.a: Create a junction table containing foreign keys to both entities. The pair often forms its primary key, with relationship attributes stored there.

mcq.why: A student can take many courses and a course can have many students.

subject: DBMS
title: 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF
learn: Normalization reduces redundancy and update anomalies by decomposing relations using dependencies. 1NF requires atomic values. 2NF means 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite candidate key. 3NF means 2NF plus no problematic transitive dependency of non-key attributes on a key. BCNF requires every determinant to be a candidate key.
example: If ENROLL(student_id, course_id, student_name, course_name, grade) has key (student_id, course_id), student_name depends only on student_id and course_name only on course_id. Those are partial dependencies, so split student and course data into separate tables.
keyPoints: Normalization is about dependencies, not simply 'more tables'.
Denormalization can intentionally add redundancy for read performance.
Always consider functional dependencies before decomposing.

interview.q: Why normalize?
interview.a: To reduce redundancy and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies while keeping dependencies clear.

mcq.q: Which normal form removes partial dependency on a composite key?
mcq.why: 2NF specifically removes partial dependencies of non-key attributes on part of a candidate key.

subject: DBMS
title: ACID and transaction basics
learn: A transaction is a logical unit of work. Atomicity means all-or-nothing. Consistency means committed transactions preserve declared rules. Isolation controls how concurrent transactions interact. Durability means committed changes survive failures.
example: Bank transfer: subtract 500 from A and add 500 to B in one transaction. If the second update fails, the first must be rolled back so money is not lost.
keyPoints: ACID properties work together.
Isolation is about concurrency; durability is about persistence after commit.
Constraints are part of database consistency but consistency is broader than constraints alone.

interview.q: What happens on rollback?
interview.a: The DBMS uses its transaction/recovery mechanisms to undo the transaction's uncommitted effects and restore the database to a valid prior state.

mcq.q: Which ACID property means committed data survives a crash?
mcq.why: Durability is the persistence guarantee after commit.

subject: DBMS
title: Isolation levels and common anomalies
learn: Concurrent transactions can cause dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. Isolation levels trade concurrency against stronger guarantees. Common SQL isolation levels are Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable. Exact behavior can vary by DBMS implementation.
example: T1 updates a balance but has not committed. If T2 reads that temporary value, T2 performed a dirty read. Read Committed prevents this class of read.
keyPoints: Serializable provides the strongest standard isolation level.
Locks, MVCC, or a combination can implement isolation.
Do not memorize only names; understand the anomaly each level permits/prevents.

interview.q: Why not always use Serializable?
interview.a: It can reduce concurrency and increase contention or retries. Applications choose an isolation level based on correctness requirements and workload.

mcq.q: Reading another transaction's uncommitted change is called?
mcq.why: A dirty read observes data that may later be rolled back.

subject: OS
title: Program vs process vs thread
learn: A program is passive code stored on disk. A process is a running program with its own execution context and resources. A thread is an execution path within a process. Threads in one process generally share its address space and resources, while each thread has its own stack and execution state.
example: Chrome is made of processes and many threads. Two threads in one process can share heap data, so communication is cheap but synchronization becomes important.
keyPoints: Process isolation is stronger than thread isolation.
Threads can improve responsiveness and parallelism.
Shared memory creates race-condition risks.

interview.q: Why are threads cheaper than processes?
interview.a: Threads usually share an existing process address space and resources, so creation and context switching can require less setup than a separate process.

mcq.q: Which is normally private to a thread?
mcq.why: Each thread has its own stack while threads normally share the process address space.

subject: OS
title: Process states and PCB
learn: A process commonly moves through New, Ready, Running, Waiting/Blocked, and Terminated states. The Process Control Block stores information the OS needs to manage it, such as process state, program counter, CPU registers, scheduling information, and memory information.
example: A running process requests disk I/O. It becomes blocked because it cannot continue until I/O completes. After completion it returns to the ready queue.
keyPoints: Ready means waiting for CPU; blocked means waiting for an event/resource.
A context switch saves one execution context and restores another.
PCB is OS bookkeeping for the process.

interview.q: Ready vs waiting?
interview.a: Ready means the process can run but is waiting for CPU scheduling. Waiting/blocked means it is waiting for an event such as I/O completion.

mcq.q: A process waiting for CPU is in which state?
mcq.why: Ready processes are eligible to be scheduled.

subject: OS
title: FCFS, SJF, SRTF, Round Robin and priority
learn: FCFS schedules in arrival order. SJF chooses the shortest estimated CPU burst and is optimal for average waiting time when burst lengths are known and the workload assumptions hold. SRTF is its preemptive version. Round Robin gives each process a time quantum. Priority scheduling chooses highest priority first and may need aging to reduce starvation.
example: With Round Robin and quantum 4 ms, a process that needs 10 ms runs for 4 ms, goes to the back of the queue, and later receives another slice.
keyPoints: Preemption can improve responsiveness.
Very small Round Robin quantum increases context-switch overhead.
Aging gradually increases priority of waiting processes.

interview.q: What is starvation?
interview.a: A process waits indefinitely because other processes keep getting scheduled first. Aging is a common mitigation.

mcq.q: Which scheduling algorithm is designed around a time quantum?
mcq.why: Round Robin repeatedly gives runnable processes a fixed time slice.

subject: OS
title: Race condition, mutex and semaphore
learn: A race condition occurs when the result depends on timing between concurrent operations on shared state. A mutex provides mutual exclusion for a critical section. A semaphore is a synchronization primitive with a counter and can coordinate access to one or more units of a resource.
example: Two threads execute counter = counter + 1. The read-modify-write sequence can interleave and lose an update. Protecting it with a mutex makes the critical section mutually exclusive.
keyPoints: Critical section is code accessing shared state that needs protection.
A binary semaphore can resemble a mutex but the ownership semantics differ.
Synchronization should protect correctness without unnecessarily serializing all work.

interview.q: Mutex vs semaphore?
interview.a: A mutex is primarily ownership-based mutual exclusion: the locker unlocks it. A semaphore represents permits/signals and can coordinate access to a pool or event.

mcq.q: What directly describes a race condition?
mcq.why: The defining problem is timing-dependent access to shared state.

subject: OS
title: Deadlock and the four necessary conditions
learn: Deadlock is a state where processes wait forever for resources held by one another. The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Breaking any one condition can prevent deadlock.
example: P1 holds lock A and waits for B while P2 holds B and waits for A. Neither can proceed. Enforcing a global lock order A then B prevents this cycle.
keyPoints: Deadlock prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery are different strategies.
Banker's algorithm is an avoidance approach using available-resource information.
Lock ordering is a practical engineering technique.

interview.q: How can lock ordering prevent deadlock?
interview.a: Give locks a global order and require threads to acquire multiple locks in that order, eliminating circular wait.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a Coffman condition?
mcq.why: No preemption, not preemption always available, is one of the four conditions.

subject: OS
title: Paging, page faults and TLB
learn: Virtual memory lets processes use virtual addresses mapped to physical frames. Paging divides virtual memory into fixed-size pages and physical memory into frames. A page fault occurs when a needed page is not currently in the required physical memory location. A TLB caches recent virtual-to-physical translations.
example: If page 7 is not present and the CPU accesses it, a page fault traps into the OS. The OS obtains the page from backing storage, possibly evicts another page, updates the page table, and retries the instruction.
keyPoints: A TLB hit avoids a page-table walk in the common case.
Page faults are much slower than ordinary memory access.
Thrashing occurs when excessive paging leaves little useful CPU work.

interview.q: Why is TLB useful?
interview.a: Address translation itself can require memory accesses. A TLB caches recent translations so many accesses avoid a full page-table lookup.

mcq.why: The Translation Lookaside Buffer caches address-translation entries.

subject: CN
title: What is a computer network?
learn: A computer network connects devices so they can exchange data using agreed protocols. Key performance terms include bandwidth (capacity), throughput (achieved transfer rate), latency (delay), and packet loss. Protocols define how data is formatted, addressed, transmitted, and interpreted.
example: When your laptop requests a web page, it creates data that is encapsulated into network messages and packets, addressed to the destination, routed through intermediate devices, and reconstructed at the receiver.
keyPoints: Bandwidth and latency are different.
A protocol is a set of communication rules.
Packets can travel through multiple networks before reaching the destination.

interview.q: Bandwidth vs latency?
interview.a: Bandwidth describes how much data a link can carry per unit time; latency describes how long it takes data to travel or a request to receive a response.

mcq.why: Latency measures communication delay.

subject: CN
title: OSI layers and practical protocol mapping
learn: OSI is a seven-layer conceptual model: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. The practical TCP/IP stack is commonly described with fewer layers. Think in terms of responsibilities rather than memorizing labels.
example: Ethernet handles link-layer framing, IP handles network-layer addressing/routing, TCP handles reliable transport, and HTTP operates at the application layer.
keyPoints: Switches primarily operate at the data-link layer.
Routers forward packets using network-layer information.
Applications usually use transport protocols such as TCP or UDP.

interview.q: Why do layers exist?
interview.a: Layering separates responsibilities, lets protocols evolve independently, and makes systems easier to reason about and troubleshoot.

mcq.q: IP is primarily associated with which layer?
mcq.why: IP provides logical addressing and routing at the network layer.

subject: CN
title: MAC address vs IP address and ARP
learn: A MAC address identifies a network interface at the local link layer. An IP address provides logical addressing used for routing between networks. ARP maps an IPv4 address to a MAC address on a local network segment.
example: Your laptop knows the server's IP but needs a local next-hop MAC to send an Ethernet frame. If that mapping is missing, it can use ARP to discover the MAC for the local destination or gateway.
keyPoints: MAC addresses are local-link identifiers; IP supports internetwork routing.
A router separates broadcast domains.
ARP is for IPv4; IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery instead.

interview.q: Does the MAC address normally route traffic across the internet?
interview.a: No. Ethernet MAC addressing is hop-local. At each routed hop, the link-layer frame can change while the IP packet is forwarded toward its destination.

mcq.why: ARP discovers the link-layer address associated with a local IPv4 address.

subject: CN
title: TCP vs UDP and the TCP handshake
learn: TCP is connection-oriented and provides reliable ordered byte-stream delivery with mechanisms for retransmission, flow control, and congestion control. UDP is connectionless and provides datagrams without TCP's built-in reliability and ordering guarantees.
example: A web request using HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 commonly runs over TCP. Real-time applications may choose UDP when application-level handling and lower protocol overhead are useful.
keyPoints: TCP reliability does not mean zero delay or zero packet loss; it hides loss through retransmission.
UDP does not mean 'unreliable application'—applications can add their own reliability.
The classic TCP connection setup uses SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.

interview.q: Why three-way handshake?
interview.a: It lets both sides establish and confirm initial sequence-number state and bidirectional reachability before normal data exchange.

mcq.q: Which provides an ordered byte stream?
mcq.why: TCP provides an ordered reliable byte-stream abstraction.

subject: CN
title: DNS, HTTP methods and status codes
learn: DNS translates names such as example.com into resource records including IP addresses. HTTP is an application protocol for request-response communication. Common methods include GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. Status codes are grouped into 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client-side errors, and 5xx server-side errors.
example: Typing a URL can trigger DNS resolution, a TCP/TLS connection when applicable, then an HTTP request such as GET /, followed by an HTTP response containing headers and content.
keyPoints: DNS can be cached at multiple levels.
GET is intended to retrieve a resource and is generally safe/idempotent.
POST is commonly used to create or trigger processing and is not generally idempotent.

interview.q: What is 404 vs 500?
interview.a: 404 means the requested resource was not found. 500 indicates an unexpected server-side error.

mcq.q: Which status family represents server errors?
mcq.why: HTTP 5xx codes indicate server-side errors.

subject: CN
title: TLS, HTTPS and certificates
learn: HTTPS is HTTP protected by TLS. TLS provides confidentiality, integrity, and authentication of the server through certificates and a trust chain. Modern TLS handshakes establish shared cryptographic keys; asymmetric cryptography is used for authentication/key establishment while symmetric cryptography efficiently protects application data.
example: A browser validates a site's certificate, performs a TLS handshake, derives session keys, and then sends HTTP data encrypted with symmetric cryptography.
keyPoints: A certificate binds a public key to an identity under a certificate authority trust model.
Encryption protects confidentiality; integrity/authentication are separate security goals.
HTTPS does not automatically make an application secure against every bug.

interview.q: Why use symmetric encryption after the handshake?
interview.a: Symmetric encryption is much faster for bulk data. Public-key operations are comparatively expensive and are mainly useful for authentication and key establishment.

mcq.q: HTTPS primarily adds what to HTTP?
mcq.why: HTTPS uses HTTP over TLS.

subject: OOP
title: Class, object, state and behavior
learn: A class defines a type's structure and behavior. An object is an instance of that class. State is represented by data/fields; behavior is represented by methods. OOP groups related state and behavior behind an abstraction.
example: A BankAccount class may contain balance and accountId plus deposit() and withdraw() methods. A particular user's account is an object with its own state.
keyPoints: A class is not itself a runtime object instance.
Encapsulation controls how state is accessed or changed.
Good objects expose meaningful behavior instead of exposing every field.

interview.q: Why encapsulate balance?
interview.a: To prevent arbitrary invalid updates and force changes through operations that can enforce business rules such as sufficient funds.

mcq.q: An object is best described as?
mcq.why: An object is a runtime instance of a class/type.

subject: OOP
title: Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism
learn: Encapsulation bundles data and operations while controlling access. Abstraction exposes essential behavior while hiding unnecessary implementation detail. Inheritance lets a type derive from another type. Polymorphism lets one interface be used with different implementations, such as method overriding through a base reference.
example: A PaymentProcessor can expose pay(amount). CardPayment and UpiPayment implement different payment behavior. Client code depends on the common abstraction rather than every implementation detail.
keyPoints: Inheritance is a reuse mechanism, not a reason to create deep hierarchies.
Runtime polymorphism commonly relies on overriding and dynamic dispatch.
Abstraction reduces coupling between callers and implementations.

interview.q: Encapsulation vs abstraction?
interview.a: Encapsulation is about bundling and controlling access to state/behavior; abstraction is about exposing the important interface while hiding implementation complexity.

mcq.why: Polymorphism allows common interfaces to work with different concrete types.

subject: OOP
title: Association, aggregation and composition
learn: Association is a general relationship between objects. Aggregation is a weaker whole-part relationship where parts can exist independently. Composition is stronger ownership: the part's lifecycle is closely tied to the whole.
example: A Teacher and Student can be associated. A Team may aggregate Players if players can exist independently. A House can compose Rooms in a model where rooms belong to that house's lifecycle.
keyPoints: These are modeling concepts; exact implementation depends on the language and design.
Composition often reduces coupling compared with inheritance.
Do not use terminology without considering object lifetimes and ownership.

interview.q: Why prefer composition over inheritance sometimes?
interview.a: Composition allows behavior to be assembled from interchangeable components and usually avoids rigid hierarchies and fragile base-class dependencies.

mcq.q: Which relationship implies stronger ownership/lifecycle dependency?
mcq.why: Composition models strong whole-part ownership.

subject: OOP
title: Compile-time vs runtime polymorphism
learn: Overloading means multiple methods share a name but have different parameter lists; the call is selected based on compile-time information in languages such as Java. Overriding means a subclass provides a new implementation of an inherited method; dynamic dispatch can select it at runtime.
example: Java add(int,int) and add(double,double) are overloads. If Animal a = new Dog(); and Dog overrides speak(), a.speak() invokes Dog's implementation at runtime.
keyPoints: Changing only return type does not create a valid Java overload.
Overriding follows language rules for visibility, final methods, static methods, and exceptions.
Python handles these ideas differently because method resolution is dynamic.

interview.q: Can static methods be overridden in Java?
interview.a: Static methods are hidden rather than dynamically overridden because static dispatch is associated with the class.

mcq.q: Which is usually resolved through dynamic dispatch?
mcq.why: Overridden instance methods can be selected at runtime based on the actual object.

subject: OOP
title: SOLID principles with practical meaning
learn: S: Single Responsibility—one reason to change. O: Open/Closed—extend behavior without modifying stable code unnecessarily. L: Liskov Substitution—subtypes should honor the expectations of the base abstraction. I: Interface Segregation—clients should not depend on methods they do not need. D: Dependency Inversion—high-level policy should depend on abstractions rather than concrete low-level details.
example: Instead of OrderService directly constructing StripePaymentGateway, depend on a PaymentGateway interface and inject the implementation. Testing becomes easier and payment providers can be swapped.
keyPoints: SOLID is guidance, not a checklist to force abstractions everywhere.
Over-abstraction can make small codebases harder to understand.
The goal is lower coupling and clearer change boundaries.

interview.q: What does dependency inversion buy you?
interview.a: It lets business logic depend on stable abstractions, making implementations replaceable and testing easier.

mcq.q: Which SOLID principle concerns clients depending on smaller interfaces?
mcq.why: Interface Segregation Principle says clients should not be forced to depend on unused methods.

subject: OOP
title: Strategy, Factory and Observer
learn: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface. Factory centralizes object creation decisions. Observer lets subscribers react when a subject publishes an event or state change.
example: A checkout system can use a PaymentStrategy for card, UPI, or wallet payments. A Factory chooses the correct strategy from configuration. An OrderPlaced event can notify email and analytics observers.
keyPoints: Patterns solve recurring design problems; they are not mandatory templates.
Prefer simple code when a pattern adds no real flexibility.
Patterns become useful when variation or decoupling is actually present.

interview.q: When would Strategy be better than a large if-else?
interview.a: When algorithms vary independently and may grow or be selected dynamically. Each strategy isolates one behavior and the caller depends on a common interface.

mcq.q: Which pattern is mainly about interchangeable algorithms?
mcq.why: Strategy packages alternative algorithms behind a common interface.

subject: SQL
title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT
learn: SELECT chooses columns or expressions. FROM chooses the source tables. WHERE filters rows before grouping. ORDER BY sorts the result. LIMIT restricts the number of returned rows in systems that support it.
example: SELECT name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 50000 ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 10; returns the ten highest-paid matching employees.
keyPoints: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.
Never rely on implicit row order without ORDER BY.
Use explicit columns instead of SELECT * in production queries when practical.

interview.q: Why is ORDER BY needed for a guaranteed order?
interview.a: SQL result sets are unordered unless an ORDER BY clause specifies the desired ordering.

mcq.why: WHERE filters rows before grouping.

subject: SQL
title: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins
learn: An INNER JOIN keeps matching rows from both sides. LEFT JOIN keeps every left row and matching right rows, using NULLs when there is no match. RIGHT is the mirror image. FULL OUTER JOIN keeps rows from both sides where supported.
example: SELECT u.name,o.id FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id=u.id; includes users who have never placed an order.
keyPoints: Put the relationship condition in ON.
A WHERE condition on a nullable right-table column can accidentally turn a LEFT JOIN into an effective INNER JOIN.
Choose joins based on the desired row preservation semantics.

interview.q: How do you find customers with no orders?
interview.a: LEFT JOIN customers to orders and filter WHERE orders.id IS NULL, assuming orders.id is non-null for real orders.

mcq.q: Which join preserves all rows from the left table?
mcq.why: LEFT JOIN preserves every left-side row.

subject: SQL
title: GROUP BY, aggregate functions and HAVING
learn: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX aggregate rows into group-level values. GROUP BY defines grouping keys. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. NULL handling differs by aggregate; for example COUNT(column) ignores NULL while COUNT(*) counts rows.
example: SELECT department, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department HAVING AVG(salary)>70000; returns departments whose average salary exceeds 70,000.
keyPoints: WHERE happens before GROUP BY; HAVING happens after grouping.
Every selected non-aggregated expression generally needs to be represented in GROUP BY, subject to DBMS-specific functional-dependency rules.
Be explicit about NULL semantics.

interview.q: WHERE vs HAVING?
interview.a: WHERE filters rows before aggregation; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

mcq.why: HAVING is evaluated against grouped/aggregated results.

subject: SQL
title: Subqueries, EXISTS and CTEs
learn: A subquery is a query nested inside another query. EXISTS tests whether a subquery returns at least one row. A CTE (WITH clause) names a query result for readability and reuse within a statement. Recursive CTEs can traverse hierarchical data in systems that support them.
example: SELECT u.id FROM users u WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id=u.id); finds users with at least one order.
keyPoints: EXISTS communicates an existence test clearly.
A CTE improves organization but is not automatically faster.
Correlated subqueries can execute conceptually per outer row; inspect the actual plan before assuming performance.

interview.q: EXISTS vs IN?
interview.a: Both can express membership/existence, but NULL semantics and optimizer behavior can differ. EXISTS is often natural when you only care whether a matching row exists.

mcq.q: What is a CTE introduced with?
mcq.why: Common table expressions use the WITH clause.

subject: SQL
title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and running totals
learn: Window functions calculate values across related rows without collapsing them into one row per group. PARTITION BY defines independent groups; ORDER BY defines the window order. ROW_NUMBER assigns unique sequence numbers. RANK gives equal values the same rank with gaps after ties.
example: ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC) can identify the highest-paid employee in each department by filtering row_number=1 in an outer query.
keyPoints: Window functions keep row detail unlike GROUP BY.
Use ROW_NUMBER for exactly one row per partition when ties must be broken deterministically.
Use RANK/DENSE_RANK when tie semantics matter.

interview.q: Top 3 salaries per department?
interview.a: Use ROW_NUMBER or RANK over PARTITION BY department ORDER BY salary DESC, then filter the computed rank in an outer query/CTE.

mcq.q: What does PARTITION BY do in a window function?
options: Splits rows into independent window groups
mcq.why: Each partition gets its own window calculation.

subject: SQL
title: Indexes, composite indexes and EXPLAIN
learn: An index is an auxiliary data structure that helps the DBMS find rows without scanning the entire table for every query. B-tree-style indexes support many equality and range searches. Composite indexes contain multiple columns, and column order matters. EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE can reveal scans, joins, estimates, and actual work depending on the DBMS.
example: If queries frequently filter WHERE user_id=? AND created_at>=?, an index beginning with (user_id, created_at) may support that access pattern well.
keyPoints: Indexes speed reads but consume storage and add write/maintenance cost.
An index is not automatically used just because it exists.
Use query plans and real workload measurements rather than guessing.

interview.q: Why can too many indexes hurt?
interview.a: Every insert/update/delete may need index maintenance, and indexes consume storage and memory/cache capacity.

mcq.q: What is EXPLAIN primarily used for?
mcq.why: EXPLAIN exposes how the DBMS plans to execute a query.

subject: DSA Fundamentals
title: Big-O, Big-Theta and space complexity
learn: Big-O gives an asymptotic upper bound, Big-Theta gives a tight asymptotic bound, and Big-Omega gives a lower bound. Ignore constant factors and lower-order terms when describing asymptotic growth. Space complexity includes additional memory used by the algorithm; clarify whether input storage is counted.
example: A loop that visits n elements is O(n). Two nested loops each running n times are O(n²). Binary search halves the search space each step, giving O(log n) time.
keyPoints: Complexity describes growth as input size increases.
Worst-case, average-case, and amortized complexity are different claims.
Amortized O(1) means the average cost over a sequence is constant even if individual operations can be expensive.

interview.q: Why is 2n+10 O(n)?
interview.a: As n grows, the linear term dominates and constant factors do not change the asymptotic growth class.

mcq.q: Binary search on a sorted array takes what time?
mcq.why: Each comparison roughly halves the remaining search interval.

subject: DSA Fundamentals
title: Arrays, hashing and prefix sums
learn: Arrays provide O(1) indexed access but inserting in the middle can require shifting elements. Hash tables provide expected O(1) lookup/insert/delete under good hashing and controlled load, though worst-case behavior can be worse. Prefix sums turn repeated range-sum queries into O(1) after O(n) preprocessing.
example: For prefix[i+1]=prefix[i]+a[i], sum(l..r)=prefix[r+1]-prefix[l]. A hash map can count frequencies or remember a value's previous index.
keyPoints: Hashing trades ordered structure for fast expected lookup.
Prefix sums are a preprocessing technique.
Always account for collision handling and worst-case complexity when explaining hashing.

interview.q: Two Sum approach?
interview.a: Scan once while storing previously seen values in a hash map. For each x, check whether target-x exists. This gives expected O(n) time and O(n) space.

mcq.why: A prefix array answers static range sums in constant time.

subject: DSA Fundamentals
title: Two pointers vs sliding window
learn: Two pointers uses two indices whose movement is justified by the structure of the problem. Sliding window is a specialized two-pointer pattern for maintaining a contiguous range and updating its state as the window expands or shrinks.
example: In a sorted array, move left/right inward for Two Sum. For longest substring without repeating characters, expand the right pointer and move left until the window is valid again.
keyPoints: Do not move pointers arbitrarily; explain the invariant.
Sliding window often reduces O(n²) substring/subarray enumeration to O(n).
Frequency maps are common window state.

interview.q: When can sliding window work?
interview.a: When the problem concerns a contiguous interval and you can update the maintained state efficiently as the left/right boundaries move.

mcq.why: The window represents a contiguous subarray or substring.

subject: DSA Fundamentals
title: Choosing stack, queue or heap
learn: A stack is LIFO and is useful for nested structure, undo operations, and monotonic-stack problems. A queue is FIFO and is central to BFS. A heap supports efficient access to a minimum or maximum element, useful for priority scheduling and top-K problems.
example: Valid parentheses uses a stack. Level-order tree traversal uses a queue. Kth largest elements can be handled with a min-heap of size k.
keyPoints: Heap insertion/removal is typically O(log n).
A binary heap is not fully sorted.
Monotonic stacks solve next-greater/next-smaller style problems.

interview.q: Why keep a heap of size k for top-k?

subject: DSA Fundamentals

Optimize memory only after the recurrence is correct.

interview.q: How do you start a DP problem?
interview.a: Ask what information completely describes a subproblem, define dp(state), derive the transition from smaller states, establish base cases, then choose an evaluation order.

mcq.why: These are the classic structural clues for dynamic programming.
